A man has sudden epigastric pain and board-like rigidity from a perforating peptic ulcer. Which site is the commonest?

choices.label: Posterior wall, first part of duodenum
Anterior wall, first part of duodenum
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which wall of the first part of the duodenum faces the free peritoneal cavity, and which wall sits over a large artery.
That choice is not right.
The posterior wall is where ulcers erode an artery and bleed. The anterior wall faces the free peritoneal cavity, so that is where the commonest perforation occurs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which wall faces the free belly before you commit.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The commonest perforation site is the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum, not the stomach.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recall the duodenum first, not the stomach.

say.text: Yes. The anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum is the commonest perforation site.
Anterior ulcers spill into the free belly; posterior ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed.

choices.label: Skip the teaching, I know the site

say.text: The anterior wall faces the free peritoneal cavity, so an ulcer that erodes full thickness spills there.
The posterior wall lies over the gastroduodenal artery, so an ulcer there erodes that artery and bleeds.
Picture a window: the front wall opens onto the free belly, the back wall opens onto a major artery.
Two duodenal ulcers. One presents with haematemesis and melaena; the other with sudden peritonitis.
Which pairing of wall, outcome and artery is right?

choices.label: Anterior ulcer bleeds from the gastroduodenal artery; posterior ulcer perforates
Posterior ulcer bleeds from the left gastric artery; anterior ulcer perforates
Posterior ulcer bleeds from the gastroduodenal artery; anterior ulcer perforates
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what lies behind each wall: one wall faces the free belly, the other faces a major artery. Which outcome goes with which?
That choice is not right.
The anterior wall faces the free peritoneal cavity and perforates; the posterior wall erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what lies behind each wall before you pair the outcome.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The posterior duodenal ulcer bleeds from the gastroduodenal artery, not the left gastric artery. The perforating ulcer is anterior.

say.text: Yes. The anterior wall faces the free belly and perforates; the posterior wall erodes the gastroduodenal artery and bleeds.
A registrar says: 'Free gas on the film means a perforated ulcer, because that is the most common cause of pneumoperitoneum.'
What does that actually let you conclude?

choices.label: Likeliest cause is an ulcer, but the picture still decides
Likeliest cause is an ulcer, so free gas means theatre
Likeliest cause is an ulcer, so no other cause matters
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read the qualifier. 'Most common' ranks causes by how often they occur. What does a frequency ranking tell you about one film?
That choice is not right.
'Most common' is a frequency word. Free gas makes an ulcer the likeliest cause, not a certain one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read 'most common' as a frequency before you commit to a cause.

say.text: That choice is not right.
'Most common' ranks causes by frequency. It does not make the ulcer the only cause, so the film and patient still need reading.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so a top-ranked cause is still one cause among several.

say.text: Yes. Perforated peptic ulcer is the most common cause of pneumoperitoneum, so it is the likeliest reading of free gas.
Keep two anchors: the commonest perforation site is the anterior first part of the duodenum, and free gas makes an ulcer the likeliest cause, not a certain one.
'Most common' is a ranking, like the most common cause of a cough. The top name is the best first guess, not the only cause.
Even a look-alike exists: the Chilaiditi sign, colon between liver and diaphragm, mimics free gas.
